stories.headline: Putin Halts Kyiv Strikes Before U.S. Envoys Arrive
stories.dek: Russian attacks on Kyiv were paused as Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reached Moscow for talks and prepared to travel on to Ukraine.
paragraphs: President Vladimir Putin ordered a pause in strikes on Kyiv before meetings in Moscow with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, according to reports. The two U.S. envoys arrived as Washington tried to restart stalled peace contacts. They are expected to travel to Kyiv after the Moscow talks.

The visit links Moscow and Kyiv in one diplomatic trip. Witkoff is President Trump’s special envoy, and Kushner is Trump’s son-in-law. Their mission, as described in reports, is to test whether direct talks can be revived after long deadlock and continued fighting between Russia and Ukraine.

It is not clear how long the pause will last, whether it covers only Kyiv, or whether either side is ready to make concessions. No agreement has been announced. The talks could lower tensions for a short time, but the wider war and any path to a settlement remain unresolved.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means a new round of U.S.-backed diplomacy is under way and may briefly reduce danger in Kyiv.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the war is ending, that strikes elsewhere have stopped, or that a peace deal is close.

cover.title: Putin Pauses Kyiv Strikes
cover.standfirst: Russian strikes on Kyiv were paused before Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow for talks with Vladimir Putin. The two U.S. envoys plan to go on to Kyiv next. The trip is meant to test whether peace talks can restart, but no deal has been announced.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: A large flat blue silhouette of Saint Sophia’s bell tower occupies the upper two-thirds, unmistakably Kyiv by its tiered belfry and small dome. Behind it, a single fluorescent-pink missile crosses right-to-left, but the narrow white gap where missile and tower nearly meet is shaped precisely like a descending passenger jet angled toward Kyiv — the flight path existing only as a temporary corridor between weapon and target. Keep the lower third largely empty off-white for type, with no extra skyline, smoke, or detail.
art.note: Tense but restrained; deep blue, black, and muted red.
art.second_beat: First you see missile and tower; a beat later the white slit resolves into the envoys’ plane, making diplomacy feel like a brief absence carved out of an ongoing attack.

stories.headline: Trump envoys arrive in Moscow for new Ukraine peace talks
stories.dek: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due in Moscow first, with a possible trip to Kyiv after Russian strikes hit Ukrainian targets.
paragraphs: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner landed in Moscow on Saturday to discuss a Trump administration proposal to end the Russia-Ukraine war. The visit comes after months of stalled diplomacy and rising civilian deaths from long-range missile and drone attacks by both sides.

Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and the war has now lasted more than four years. Trump says the envoys will test whether a peace deal is possible. After Moscow, they are expected to go to Kyiv, though the plan has shifted and the Ukraine leg was still uncertain on Friday.

It is not clear what the U.S. proposal contains or whether it asks Ukraine to give up territory. It is also unclear whether the envoys will meet Vladimir Putin, whether they will fly into closed Ukrainian airspace, and whether any temporary ceasefire will hold during the talks.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means the United States is making another direct attempt to restart talks between Moscow and Kyiv.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean a ceasefire or peace deal exists yet, and fighting is still continuing on the ground.

cover.title: US Envoys Reach Moscow
cover.standfirst: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday with a Trump-backed plan to end the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year. They are expected to travel on to Kyiv on Sunday if security allows, after Russian strikes hit Kyiv airports and a civilian site in the Dnipro region.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: A nearly empty cover: from the upper left, a thin red in-flight route line curves diagonally down toward Moscow. In the last third it turns into a jagged crack in concrete, splitting the pale ground as it reaches a small black jet silhouette descending over the unmistakable onion domes and wall of the Kremlin; just before the city, a faint unresolved fork in the line peels westward and dies out. Keep the lower third quiet and open for type; use only black, red and a pale ground, with the Kremlin silhouette specific enough to read instantly as Moscow.
art.note: Grave and spare, with deep reds, black, and cold grey-blue.
art.second_beat: First it reads as envoys flying in for talks; a beat later the route is also a fracture, so diplomacy is shown arriving along a ceasefire already breaking and with Kyiv still unresolved.

stories.headline: US strikes hit three Iranian oil carriers in Indian Ocean
stories.dek: The attack widened a fight over Iranian shipping and raised new fears for oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
paragraphs: The US military said it struck three Iranian crude oil carriers in the Indian Ocean. The reported attack came as fighting between Washington and Tehran sharpened around the Strait of Hormuz. Hitting oil carriers goes beyond earlier pressure on shipping and directly targets Iran’s export trade.

The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s main routes for oil and gas. Iran has faced a US naval blockade on parts of its shipping, and both sides have traded strikes in recent weeks. Any attack on tankers raises the risk of disrupted energy supplies and wider military retaliation.

It is still unclear how badly the vessels were damaged, whether there were casualties, and how Iran will respond. Traders and airlines are watching for any Iranian move to restrict airspace or shipping. Official statements from Tehran and Washington could quickly change the risk of further escalation.
stories.changes: This raises the chance of higher fuel prices, shipping delays, and wider travel disruption if the conflict spreads.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the Strait of Hormuz is closed now or that a broader regional war is certain.

cover.title: US Hits Iranian Oil Carriers
cover.standfirst: The US military said it struck three Iranian crude oil carriers in the Indian Ocean as tensions with Iran rose around the Strait of Hormuz. The attack puts Iran’s export route in the firing line. Markets, shippers and airlines are now watching for retaliation or fresh limits on airspace and sea traffic.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Seen from above, a single vast black oil slick fills the page, its ragged edge spreading across open sea. Cut out of that slick in stark white negative space is the unmistakable narrow shape of the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf beyond, so the stain itself becomes the threatened chokepoint; near the upper edge, three tiny red tanker silhouettes are caught mid-strike, breaking apart and burning, while the lower third remains mostly clear water for type.
art.note: Severe and spare; deep navy, black, and one hard red-orange accent
art.second_beat: First you see an expanding spill from the attacks; a beat later you realise the white void inside it is the map of Hormuz, turning damage at sea into a threat to the whole passage.

stories.headline: US disables three Iranian tankers after missiles hit Navy ships
stories.dek: The strikes in the Strait of Hormuz damaged ship systems without sinking the vessels, after Iran fired missiles at two US warships.
paragraphs: The US military said it disabled three oil tankers linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard on September 5 in the Strait of Hormuz. The action came after Iranian forces fired missiles at two US Navy warships. US officials said they used precision strikes to stop the tankers without causing major oil spills.

The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important oil routes. About one-fifth of global petroleum use passes through it. The US says Iran and the Revolutionary Guard have attacked ships and US targets in the region through 2026, while Washington has struck dozens of Iranian military assets and tightened pressure on oil exports.

It is still unclear whether Iran will answer with more attacks on warships, tankers or ports. Commercial traffic is still moving, but under heavier naval protection and higher insurance costs. The immediate danger is a wider fight that disrupts oil shipments, even if these three vessels stay afloat.
stories.changes: Oil shipping through the Gulf now carries more military risk, which can feed into fuel prices and insurance costs far from the region.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the Strait has closed or that global oil supplies have stopped moving today.

cover.title: US Hits Iranian Oil Tankers
cover.standfirst: The US said it disabled three Iranian tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on September 5 after Iranian missiles targeted two Navy warships. The ships were damaged but not sunk, and no casualties were reported. Oil traffic is still moving under tighter naval escort as markets watch for Iran’s next step.

art.label: Maximalist doodle
art.concept: A single thick white contrail curves diagonally across a dark sea and, without changing style, becomes the exposed hose-and-pipe run along the deck of an oil tanker threading the Strait of Hormuz. At one end of the curve sit two tiny, unmistakable US destroyers with fading launch smoke; along the same line, three tankers in convoy are the only ships whose wakes abruptly stop and whose hulls cant out of lane, while the surrounding merchant traffic continues normally. Keep the lower third mostly open water with only a few faint route lines so type can sit there cleanly.
art.note: Grave, high-contrast, with deep navy, black, rust red and a small harsh white.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a clean shipping route; a beat later the same line snaps into a missile path, making oil flow and attack literally the same contour.

stories.headline: Masked anti-migrant protest blocks traffic at Dover ferry port
stories.dek: Hundreds in balaclavas halted vehicles for hours at Britain’s main ferry terminal before police restored normal traffic.
paragraphs: Hundreds of anti-migrant protesters blocked traffic at the Port of Dover on Saturday, stopping ferry movement between Britain and France for several hours. Video showed masked demonstrators in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats." The protest came as small-boat migration remains a live political issue despite a recent fall in crossings.

Dover is Britain’s busiest international ferry port. In summer it handles about 15,000 passengers a day and more than a third of the country’s trade with the European Union. Crossings of the English Channel by migrants fell 40% from January to August 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier.

Police said they were engaging with protesters and that normal traffic had resumed. The government condemned the disruption but repeated that peaceful protest is protected. It is still unclear whether arrests will follow, whether more actions are planned, and whether the protest will deepen pressure on the government’s migration policy.
stories.changes: If you use Dover, this shows how quickly a political protest there can disrupt travel and freight for ordinary passengers and drivers.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Channel crossings are rising again, or that Britain’s border system suddenly stopped working on Saturday.

cover.title: Masked Protest Blocks Dover
cover.standfirst: Hundreds of anti-migrant protesters in balaclavas blocked traffic at the Port of Dover on Saturday, halting ferry movement between Britain and France for hours. Police later restored normal traffic. The government condemned the disruption at the port that carries 15,000 summer passengers a day and a large share of UK-EU trade.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: Show the Dover port road barrier in a stark black-and-white cutout, dropping diagonally across the frame over a flat hazard-orange ground. But the barrier arm is not a plank: it is a single fused bar made from a row of balaclava-covered heads and shoulders, rigid and mechanical, descending to stop two tiny waiting car silhouettes; keep the lower third mostly open road for type, and add only the minimum port cues — a clipped white ferry hull and chalk cliff edge high in the background — so Dover is unmistakable without clutter.
art.note: Tense, public-facing, with flat reds, navy, grey, and ferry white.
art.second_beat: First you see a port barrier stopping traffic; a beat later you realise the protesters have become the machinery that controls who moves and who doesn’t.

stories.headline: Pogacar ends season after Vuelta crash and neck fracture
stories.dek: The Slovenian champion will miss the World Championships after surgery on a broken collarbone, concussion and a stable neck fracture.
paragraphs: Tadej Pogacar will not race again this season after injuries from his crash on stage eight of the Vuelta a Espana. His team announced the decision now because his recovery will continue through the autumn. He had surgery on a broken collarbone and also suffered concussion and a stable neck fracture.

Pogacar, 27, is one of cycling's biggest riders and has won the Tour de France five times. He crashed out of the Vuelta while leading the race and lost his chance to add that title to his Giro d'Italia win. He will now miss the World Championships in Montreal and October races in Europe.

It is not clear when he will race again, beyond the team saying it will not set a return date before next season. The team also said Pogacar has signed a two-year contract extension through 2032. His recovery, and how quickly he can resume full training, remain the main unknowns.
stories.changes: Fans will not see Pogacar defend his world title or race again this year.
stories.unchanged: This does not end his career, and his team says the focus is a full recovery rather than a rushed return.

cover.title: Pogacar Out For Season
cover.standfirst: Tadej Pogacar will not race again in 2026 after his Vuelta a Espana crash last month. The Slovenian suffered a broken collarbone, concussion and a stable neck fracture, and had surgery. He will miss the World Championships in Montreal and his other autumn races while he recovers.

art.label: Comic absurd
art.concept: On a steep Vuelta-style mountain descent, show the red leader’s bike in a violent front-end skid, but where the front wheel should be there is a white medical neck brace taking the load against the road, visibly buckling and scraping as the bike pitches forward. Keep the rider mostly out of frame — just the red leader’s jersey and arms being thrown ahead — and strip the scene to road, a hint of barrier, and open lower-third asphalt for type; add only two or three tiny bandage strips flicking off the brace like tyre spray so the substitution lands a beat later.
art.note: Quiet, bruised mood; dusty reds, road grey and pale medical white.
art.second_beat: First you read a crash; a moment later you realise the front wheel has become the neck brace, turning the injury into the mechanism of the fall and making this story unmistakable.

stories.headline: Sara Duterte posts bail after arrest order in threat case
stories.dek: The Philippine vice president paid 360,000 pesos after a court ordered her arrest over alleged threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
paragraphs: Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail on Saturday after a court ordered her arrest a day earlier. She faces three counts of grave threats over remarks in 2024 about having President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and two others killed. The case now moves forward in court.

Duterte denies threatening the president. She says she was speaking about her own safety during a worsening political feud. She and Marcos won office together in 2022, but their alliance broke down. She is also facing an impeachment trial in the Senate over separate allegations.

It is not yet clear whether prosecutors can win a conviction or how fast the case will move. A conviction could bar Duterte from future public office, including a 2028 presidential run. She remains vice president for now, and the larger Marcos-Duterte power struggle is still unfolding.
stories.changes: An ordinary reader should now see Duterte's clash with Marcos as a live court case, not only a political feud.
stories.unchanged: This does not remove Duterte from office today, and it does not settle whether she will be convicted or impeached.

cover.title: Duterte Posts Bail
cover.standfirst: Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte posted 360,000 pesos bail in Manila on Saturday after a court ordered her arrest over alleged threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his wife and an ally. She denies the charges. The criminal case and her separate impeachment trial will now continue.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a plain studio sweep in a single muted colour, place a clear tamper-evident evidence bag slightly off-centre in the upper half of frame, leaving the entire lower third empty for type. Inside the sealed bag: one tight rubber-banded bundle of Philippine peso notes and, pressed visibly against the plastic, a small polished vice-presidential seal-like medallion or office insignia shape with no readable text; light it flat and forensic, with just enough crinkle in the plastic to show the bag has been closed around both objects. Keep everything else out: no extra props, no labels, no courtroom cues.
art.note: Tense, public, procedural; red, black and off-white palette.
art.second_beat: First it reads as bail cash bagged as evidence; a beat later, the office itself appears trapped inside the money and the case.

stories.headline: Dark matter detector logged one unexplained event deep underground
stories.dek: The LZ experiment in South Dakota saw a single xenon strike in 2023 that does not match any known particle signal.
paragraphs: Scientists running the LZ dark matter detector said they found one strange particle event in data from 2023 and decided to publish it now. The signal came from nearly a mile underground and does not fit any interaction the team expected to see in the detector.

LZ is a seven-ton tank of liquid xenon in a former South Dakota gold mine. It is built to catch rare collisions between ordinary atoms and dark matter, the unseen material thought to make up most of the universe's mass and help hold galaxies together.

No one knows what caused this event. It could be a statistical fluke, an unknown background effect, or a sign of physics beyond standard dark matter models. The result falls far short of the proof scientists require, so other detectors will now try to check for the same kind of hit.
stories.changes: For now, it means dark matter searches may need to watch for rarer, higher-energy signals than many standard models predicted.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean dark matter has been discovered, and it does not change everyday life or settled physics yet.

cover.title: LZ Detector Sees Strange Hit
cover.standfirst: At the LZ dark matter detector in South Dakota, physicists found one unexplained particle event in 2023 inside seven tons of liquid xenon nearly a mile underground. The signal is too weak to count as a discovery. Teams at other detectors, including XENONnT and PandaX, will now look for a matching event.

art.label: Minimal mark
art.concept: A stark white cover with a single black silhouette hanging high and slightly off-centre: at first glance it is the familiar mine elevator cage descending into a shaft, suspended by one thin cable from the top edge. On the second look, the 'cage' is unmistakably the LZ detector tank — a clean cylindrical vessel with the proportions and domed ends of the xenon chamber, not a lift — dropping into empty white depth; keep the entire lower third clear and untouched for type.
art.note: Quiet, precise, subterranean mood; deep charcoal, slate, and cold xenon blue.
art.second_beat: First it reads as the old Homestake mine lift going down; then the substituted form lands, and the detector itself becomes the thing lowered into the underground unknown to catch one inexplicable strike.

stories.headline: Isar Aerospace set for new orbital launch attempt from Norway
stories.dek: The German company's Spectrum rocket is due to lift off tonight from Andoya with six payloads after months of delays and one failed debut.
paragraphs: Isar Aerospace is due to try again today to launch its Spectrum rocket from Andoya Space Center in northern Norway. If it reaches orbit, it would be the first rocket to do so from European soil. The launch window opens at 10 p.m. local time.

Spectrum is a two-stage rocket built by the German company Isar for small and medium-size satellites. Its first flight, from the same site in March 2025, failed less than a minute after liftoff. Investigators blamed a vent valve opening and a loss of attitude control.

It is not clear whether Spectrum can complete the full mission after earlier scrubs for valve, leak, weather and fluid-system problems. This flight carries five cubesats and one scientific experiment, so the test now matters to customers as well as to Isar.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this could open a new European launch option for small satellites and the services that depend on them.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Europe suddenly has routine independent access to space; one successful flight would be an early step, not a finished system.

cover.title: Spectrum Launches From Norway
cover.standfirst: Isar Aerospace plans to launch its 28-meter Spectrum rocket from Andoya Space Center in northern Norway at 10 p.m. local time today. The German company is carrying five cubesats and one scientific experiment. If the rocket reaches orbit, it will be the first to do so from European soil.

art.label: Decorative flat
art.concept: Show one Andoya launch in two stacked states using the same stripped-down coastal geometry so the place is unmistakable: low island, launch pad, bands of dark sea and pale Nordic sky. In the lower half, Spectrum’s first attempt is already going wrong — the rocket has just lifted but is tilting off-axis, its exhaust breaking into ragged fragments; in the upper half, tonight’s attempt rises from the same pad dead straight, clean plume, climbing into open sky. Keep the lower third quiet with only the pad, shoreline and a tight cluster of six tiny payload shapes waiting below the divide; above, those six reappear separated as a delicate trail following the successful rocket.
art.note: Tense and clean; cold blues and blacks with a hard white-orange engine flare.
art.second_beat: First read: failure versus success in the same place; second beat: the six payloads move from a waiting cluster below to a released trail above, turning the image into this specific delayed second attempt.

stories.headline: White House review begins for SEC rewrite on crypto custody
stories.dek: A new SEC rule draft would spell out how advisers and investment companies must hold digital assets after an earlier proposal was dropped.
paragraphs: A rewritten SEC rule on custody of digital assets has entered White House review, a late step before a federal proposal is released. The draft would apply to investment advisers and investment companies. It comes after the SEC withdrew a separate 2023 plan and started over on this part of crypto regulation.

Custody rules govern who can hold client assets and what safeguards they must use. For crypto, that has been a basic problem because tokens can sit in digital wallets, move across blockchains, and be lost through bad controls or theft. Advisers and funds have lacked clear federal guidance on what counts as proper custody.

The draft text is not public yet, so key details are still unknown. It is not clear which digital assets would be covered, what firms would qualify as custodians, or how strict the operational requirements would be. White House review can also lead to changes before the proposal is formally published.
stories.changes: If you invest through a fund or adviser, the government may soon set clearer rules on where your crypto can be held.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean crypto is newly approved, banned, or made safer overnight for people buying tokens on their own.

cover.title: SEC Rewrites Crypto Custody
cover.standfirst: A new SEC draft on crypto custody has reached White House review in Washington, a key step before publication. The rule would cover investment advisers and investment companies and explain how digital assets should be held. It follows the withdrawal of a separate 2023 proposal. The text is still not public.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a flat pale blue seamless, stage a small matte-black hardware crypto wallet halfway jammed into a narrow transparent document sleeve attached to a crisp stack of official-looking filing papers with ruled lines, boxes and a blind embossed seal shape but no readable text. The wallet is visibly too thick: the plastic sleeve bows outward, the top sheet buckles, and one corner catches as if the paperwork itself is trying and failing to hold the asset; keep the action in the upper half so the lower third stays clean for type.
art.note: Cool, official mood; gray, silver, and muted blue palette.
art.second_beat: First read: crypto and official custody paperwork; second beat: the asset physically does not fit the container, turning the custody-rule problem into one stuck, failing action.
